body.heading: A sequence built by adding
paragraphs: The Fibonacci sequence starts 1, 1, and then every new number is the sum of the two before it: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34. It is one of the easiest sequences to extend and one of the hardest to stop thinking about.

It is named after Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, who described it in 1202 in a puzzle about breeding rabbits. The sequence turned out to matter far beyond rabbits — especially where living things grow by adding new parts at a steady angle.

body.heading: Where the numbers show up
paragraphs: Look at a pinecone from below and you will see spirals running in two directions. Count them, and the counts are very often neighbouring Fibonacci numbers — 8 spirals one way and 13 the other is a common find. Sunflower heads do the same on a grander scale, often with 34 and 55, or 55 and 89 spirals.

This pattern in plant growth is called phyllotaxis. Packing seeds at a particular angle — about 137.5 degrees, the 'golden angle' — lets a flower fit the most seeds with the least waste, and Fibonacci numbers fall out of that geometry naturally.

body.heading: Go and count
paragraphs: On your next walk, collect a pinecone and count its spirals both ways, marking each spiral with a dot of pen as you count it so you do not chase the same one twice. Write down what you find, even if it is not a Fibonacci number — honest counting beats a good story.

Then try a pineapple: its diamond pattern spirals in three directions, and the counts are often 8, 13 and 21. Nature is not following a rule book; it is solving a packing problem, and the same solution keeps appearing.

takeaway: Add the last two numbers to get the next — then go outside and count spirals: growing things keep using the same shortlist.
